title: How To Make Your Consequences Matter To Students
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Responding to the common teacher complaint that 'my students don't care about consequences,' Linsin argues the real issue is not the students but the meaning attached to the consequences themselves. He offers three strategies: clearly explaining exactly where the rule boundaries lie so breaking them is always a conscious choice, explaining why rules exist by citing psychologist Ellen Langer's research on the persuasive power of the word 'because,' and explaining how misbehavior tramples on classmates' right to learn, building empathy in the process. He closes by naming a fourth, overarching factor—students' genuine love of the class itself—as the ultimate multiplier that makes any consequence, even a mild warning, land with real weight.
points: Reframes the complaint 'my students don't care about consequences' as really being about the meaning attached to them, not the students themselves.
Recommends explaining precisely where rule boundaries lie so every instance of misbehavior is a conscious student choice.
Cites Harvard psychologist Ellen Langer's research showing the word 'because' significantly increases compliance with requests.
Advises explaining how misbehavior harms classmates' right to learn, in order to build empathy in rule-breakers.
Names students' genuine love of the class as the ultimate factor that makes consequences, even mild ones, effective.
quotes: It’s said as a statement of fact, as if an unchanging part of who the students are. But if this were really true, if repercussions for misbehavior mean nothing to them, then the game is essentially over.

In her pioneering work, Harvard research psychologist Ellen Langer showed that when we use the word ‘because’ and attach a reason to our requests—even if the reason makes little sense—it results in significantly greater compliance.
The third key is to show how disruptions, interruptions, impoliteness, and the like trample on the right of every student to learn and enjoy school.
When your students love being part of your class, when they like you and look forward to coming to school, then you have the keys to the kingdom.
It’s the answer, the solution, the secret to effective classroom management.
